entityDossier.whatItIs: The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office is the Pentagon body designated in July 2022 as the Department's authoritative office for unidentified anomalous phenomena. It was created under section 1683 of the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act, sits under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, and absorbed the Navy's Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. It publishes the statutory annual UAP report, runs a secure reporting mechanism for current and former government personnel, and produced the Historical Record Report.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: AARO is the single point through which every UAP record, contract and data holding in the Department of Defense was ordered to flow, which makes it either the instrument of disclosure or the instrument of consolidation, and the record supports the second reading. The office was given, by its own account, unrestricted statutory access to compartmented and special access material, then used that access to produce a report clearing the Department of every allegation made against it. Its own numbers show what the reporting channel actually does: of 262 people who came forward in a single year, 255 were declared out of scope and 7 were judged worth interviewing. Witnesses under oath before the House Oversight Committee have described being targeted after providing classified testimony, and one described a session he understood to be with AARO leadership as an effort to attack the credibility of UAP witnesses. AARO is on this map not as an arbiter but as a party: it holds the custody, it wrote the exoneration, and it decides who counts as a witness.
entityDossier.narrative:
AARO exists because Congress forced it into existence. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA required the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to stand up an office with a scope broader than the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group that the Deputy Secretary had created in November 2021. On 15 July 2022 Deputy Secretary Kathleen Hicks signed the memorandum that renamed and expanded AOIMSG into AARO. That memorandum is the founding document and it is worth reading for what it actually does. It makes AARO the authoritative office for UAP and UAP-related activities for the whole Department. It orders the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAP Task Force and transfer its data, analysis and other relevant material. And it contains the sentence that matters most for this board: any DoD Component acting on behalf of the UAPTF, or who has data, analysis, contracts, or other material related to UAP, will immediately synchronize their efforts with the AARO.

That is a consolidation order. In a Department where the argument is that recovered material and its associated paperwork have been dispersed across contractors and unacknowledged compartments, an instruction that all UAP data, analysis and contracts route to a single office under USD(I&S) is the sort of instruction that can be read two ways. It is the necessary precondition for an honest accounting. It is also the necessary precondition for a controlled one.

AARO's first director was Sean Kirkpatrick, previously chief scientist at the Defense Intelligence Agency's Missile and Space Intelligence Center. He retired on 1 December 2023 having largely completed the Historical Record Report that his office published the following March. He publicly characterised David Grusch's allegations while, by his own later account, never having interviewed him. Grusch's position is that AARO never contacted him. Whichever account is correct, the resulting document is an investigation of a whistleblower's claims conducted without the whistleblower. Jon Kosloski, from the National Security Agency, took over in late 2024.

The office's own annual reporting is the best evidence about how the reporting channel functions. Under section 3373b of title 50, AARO hosts a secure mechanism for people claiming first-hand knowledge of a US Government UAP-related programme dating back to 1945. In the FY2025 report AARO discloses that between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, 262 individuals used it. AARO determined 255 were out of scope. Seven warranted a request for a follow-on interview. That is a 97 percent rejection rate applied by the office whose own conduct is the subject of many of the allegations. The same report states, in language AARO chose, that the office is authorised by law to receive all UAP-related information at any level of classification regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs, and that generally no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving it. AARO therefore claims the access and simultaneously reports that almost nobody who comes to it has anything worth hearing.

The FY2025 report contains a second internal tension that a hostile reader should sit with. It states flatly that to date no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. Two sentences later it states that AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG, drawing on established procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel. An office that has found nothing is building a custody chain for the nothing it has found.

The performance record is poor by the Department's own inspector general's measure. DODIG-2023-109, whose unclassified summary was released on 24 January 2024, found the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP, had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan, and had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands. The Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report.

The delivery record is worse. Volume II of the Historical Record Report, covering interviews and research from 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024, was promised in Volume I under a deadline set in section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA. By late February 2026 it had not appeared, the FY2025 annual report had not appeared, the deputy director post was vacant, and Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough, asked why AARO had not published or briefed in over a year, told DefenseScoop the office had nothing to announce at this time. Gough did confirm that AARO had been examining over 2,000 UAP cases, roughly 1,000 of which lacked sufficient data and sat in an active archive. When the FY2025 report finally issued, it carried document number 26-P-0880 and a Department of War letterhead, with an information cut-off of 30 May 2025.

The strongest single item against AARO is in its own Volume I. The report concedes that in 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and that the programme was later disestablished for lack of merit. AARO's framing is that the compartment was unwarranted and empty. The fact remains that a compartment was stood up to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and the office that told us so is the office that closed it.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, Volume I, is a 63-page unclassified report published by AARO on 8 March 2024 under a congressional mandate to document the US Government's UAP record back to 1945. It covers the period from 1945 to 31 October 2023 and was largely prepared under director Sean Kirkpatrick before his retirement on 1 December 2023. A Volume II covering 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024 was promised and has not appeared.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Volume I is the government's formal written denial that a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering programme exists, and as such it is the central artifact of the concealment argument rather than a rebuttal to it. It is an investigation of roughly thirty interviewees conducted without interviewing the most prominent complainant, written by the office whose own conduct several of the allegations concern, and published by the same office that decides which claims are in scope. Its own text concedes that an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program had its scope expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering, which is the single most consequential sentence any US government UAP document has ever contained. It disposes of the rest of the record by attributing it to circular reporting among a group of people who worked on a real, congressionally funded Defense Intelligence Agency programme. Volume I is on this map because it is the document a concealment effort would have to produce, and because the promised second half has never arrived.
entityDossier.narrative:
The FY2023 NDAA, enacted December 2022, required AARO to produce a written report on the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena going back to 1 January 1945. AARO split the deliverable. Volume I would carry findings from 1945 to 31 October 2023. Volume II would carry anything derived from interviews and research completed between 1 November 2023 and 15 April 2024, on a date set by section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA. Volume I went to Congress in the first week of March 2024 and to the public on 8 March. Volume II has not been published.

The methodology is stated plainly in the report and is the first thing a hostile reader should notice. AARO reviewed official investigatory efforts since 1945, researched classified and unclassified archives, partnered with IC and DoD officials responsible for controlled and special access programme oversight, and conducted approximately 30 interviews. Thirty interviews is the entire human-source basis for a report covering seventy-eight years. AARO categorised the interviewees into tiers, with Tier 1 being those referred to AARO after speaking with Members of Congress or congressional staff. The report then states that none of the interviewees had firsthand knowledge of these programmes, that they were not approved for access and did not work on these efforts, and that this likely resulted in misinterpretation.

The findings are absolute in tone. AARO found no evidence that any USG investigation, academic-sponsored research, or official review panel has confirmed that any sighting of a UAP represented extraterrestrial technology. AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology. AARO has found no evidence of any authentic UAP-related NDA or other evidence threatening death or violence for disclosing UAP information. AARO has found no evidence that U.S. companies ever possessed off-world technology; the report says executives, scientists and chief technology officers of named companies met the Director of AARO and denied on the record ever having recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered such technology. A metal sample obtained from a private UAP investigating organisation and the US Army is assessed as a manufactured terrestrial alloy of magnesium, zinc and bismuth with trace elements including lead.

Against that, the report contains admissions its authors evidently regarded as harmless. It states that in 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering, that the programme never recovered or reverse-engineered anything, and that it was disestablished for lack of merit. It states that KONA BLUE was a Prospective Special Access Program proposed to the Department of Homeland Security, never approved, whose supporters never provided empirical evidence. It states that on 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III asking that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program and that Lynn declined on the recommendation of Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence James Clapper. It states that a named former CIA official signed a memo rejecting the claim that he had managed the movement of and experimentation on off-world technology, which means AARO went to that official and obtained a denial rather than a record. It states that an alleged 1961 Special National Intelligence Estimate circulating online is inauthentic.

The report's explanatory theory is that the modern allegations are, in large part, the result of circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case despite the lack of any evidence, and that these individuals have been involved in various UAP-related endeavours since at least 2009, many of them connected to the cancelled DIA programme and the failed attempt to re-establish it under DHS as KONA BLUE. This is a genetic argument. It explains the allegations by the identity of the people making them rather than by testing what they allege, and it does so while conceding that the DIA programme was real, congressionally funded, and terminated over the objections of a sitting Senate Majority Leader.

The report also records lines of effort that are useful to this board regardless of its conclusions. AARO partnered with the archives of the Defense Intelligence Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the National Security Agency, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the Services and the Combatant Commands, and with the US National Archives on locating UAP data. It interviewed five former Air Force members who served in and around intercontinental ballistic missile silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth and other sites regarding a narrative of UAP over nuclear facilities. It records Captain Edward Ruppelt of Project GRUDGE noting concentrations of cases in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area, Oak Ridge, White Sands, Strategic Air Command locations, ports and industrial sites.

One correction this board has already logged belongs here permanently. A full-text search of the released Volume I returns no occurrence of the term YANKEE BLUE. The widely repeated claim that AARO conceded that programme in Volume I does not survive a check of the document.

Volume I should be read as a primary record of what the United States Government said in March 2024, which is exactly the tier at which it belongs. It is not a primary record of the facts it asserts, and its authors have never produced the second half.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Department of Defense, renamed the Department of War by executive action in 2025, is the cabinet department that has run every official US government UAP investigation from Project SIGN in December 1947 to AARO today. It holds the special access programme architecture, the counterintelligence organisations that respond to incursions on military installations, and the security review office that clears what its personnel may say in public. It is the institution against which the legacy programme allegation is principally made.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The Department has controlled every official UAP investigation for seventy-nine years and, by its own inspector general's finding, still had no coordinated approach and no comprehensive response plan eighteen months after Congress ordered it to build one. Its structure gives it the two things a concealed recovery programme requires: an unacknowledged special access programme system whose existence need not be disclosed, and counterintelligence organisations designated as the first responders to any anomalous incursion on any installation or range. Congress has twice legislated as though it believes unreported UAP compartments exist, first by giving AARO statutory access notwithstanding all access controls, then by forbidding the expenditure of funds on UAP-related special access activity not reported to the intelligence committees. A former DoD official who managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council testified under oath that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies and that the effort is hidden from elected representatives. The Department's own Historical Record Report concedes that a controlled access compartment was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Department's UAP history is documented by its own inspector general. The first official DoD UAP activity was PROJECT SIGN, established by the Air Force Chief of Staff in December 1947. From 1947 to 1949 Air Force personnel investigated 243 reported sightings. In 1952 the Air Force Director of Intelligence initiated PROJECT BLUE BOOK, which investigated more than 12,000 sightings before its termination in 1969. Then, in the inspector general's own words, the DoD did not officially look at UAP again until mid-2000, when select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme to study UAP under the direction of the Defense Intelligence Agency. That sentence is worth pausing on. The Department's own watchdog records that the resumption of UAP work was not a Departmental decision at all. It was a congressional earmark inserted over the Department's disinterest, and when the Senate Majority Leader asked for it to be made a Special Access Program in June 2009 the Deputy Secretary of Defense declined on the advice of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence.

That forty-year gap is the load-bearing claim of the official account and the weakest point in it. The Department asks the public to accept that between BLUE BOOK's closure in 1969 and AAWSAP's standup in 2008 it did nothing on the subject at all, in the same period in which it was operating an unacknowledged special access programme architecture whose whole purpose is that its contents cannot be inferred from budget documents or organisation charts.

Congress does not appear to accept it. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA forced the creation of an office. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the creation of a reporting mechanism usable notwithstanding non-disclosure agreements and free from reprisal. Section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the historical report. Section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA went further and prohibited the use of authorised funds for any special access or restricted access programme activity relating to UAP that has not been reported to the congressional committees by the Director of National Intelligence, and extended the restriction to contractor Independent Research and Development. Legislators do not write funding prohibitions against activities they believe do not exist.

The Deputy Secretary's July 2022 establishment memorandum is the Department's own consolidation instrument. It made AARO the authoritative office for all UAP and UAP-related activities, disestablished the Navy task force, and directed every DoD component holding UAP data, analysis, contracts or other material to synchronise immediately with AARO. If material and paperwork from a legacy programme existed anywhere in the Department, that memorandum is the order that would have moved it, and it moved it into an office reporting to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security.

The inspector general's evaluation, DODIG-2023-109, is the best independent measure of the Department's conduct. Its unclassified summary, released 24 January 2024, found that the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP; that DoD components had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands, the organisations actually responsible for detecting and preventing threats against the United States; that components had developed varying informal processes; and that the Department had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan. The evaluation notes that the Military Services and counterintelligence organisations had sent some UAP incident reports to AARO but that the Department does not formally require them to do so. It also records that the Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report. That is three of the Department's most senior officials refusing to go on the record with the inspector general on this subject.

The response architecture matters as much as the analytic one. AARO's FY2025 report states that the military Services' counterintelligence, law enforcement and security agencies are the cognizant authorities responsible for responding to UAP incidents and incursions on all installations and ranges, and that AARO aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025. entityDossier.narrative:
In 2008 DIA posted a solicitation and awarded a contract to Bigelow Aerospace for what became the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program. The money came from Senate-directed appropriations rather than a Departmental requirement, a point the DoD Inspector General records plainly when it notes that the Department did not officially look at UAP again after Blue Book until select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme under DIA's direction. The programme ran from 2008 through 2012 in its various forms and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents covering advanced propulsion, warp drive metrics, traversable wormholes, metamaterials, invisibility cloaking, high energy laser weapons, and biological effects of anomalous exposure. DIA transmitted the list of titles and principal authors to Congress in January 2018.

AARO's own account of AAWSAP, in Historical Record Report Volume I and in its standalone KONA BLUE paper, is more useful to this board than AARO seems to have realised. It confirms the programme was managed by DIA from 2009 to 2012 and funded through congressional earmarks with Bigelow Aerospace as prime contractor. It confirms the stated purpose was investigating next-generation aerospace technologies across twelve specific areas including advanced lift, propulsion, unconventional materials and controls, and signature reduction. It then states that although investigating UFO or UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organisation conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA programme manager, and that this research included reviewing new cases and older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.

That sentence is the whole argument in miniature. A defence intelligence agency programme, funded outside the normal requirements process, with a programme manager who authorised his contractor to run field investigation teams and to propose materials exploitation laboratories for recovered UFO material. AARO's framing is that DIA did not seek nor specifically authorise this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract, which is an attempt to place the agency at arm's length from its own programme manager. It does not work. A contract managed by an agency employee, funded by an agency line, delivering to an agency archive, is the agency's programme.

The escalation attempt is documented. On 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Lynn declined on the recommendation of then Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence James Clapper, who advised that the designation was not justified. Read against the concealment thesis, a request for SAP status is a request for a compartment in which recovered material could lawfully be held without disclosure, and the refusal is the point at which the effort had to find another home.

It found one, briefly. AARO's KONA BLUE paper states that when DIA cancelled AAWSAP/AATIP, several individuals involved advocated that the Department of Homeland Security take the effort over and fund a new version under the code name KONA BLUE. In 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology established KONA BLUE as a Prospective Special Access Program based on claims that relevant information and material existed and required this level of protection. Six months later the Deputy Secretary of DHS disapproved it and directed immediate termination. AARO's insistence that no data or material was ever transferred to DHS is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that a Presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Under Secretary stood up a prospective compartment on the strength of a representation that material existed.

The custody question is settled by AARO's own words. Its KONA BLUE paper states that information associated with the activities conducted under the auspices of AAWSAP/AATIP remains within DIA's archived holdings. Whatever the thirty-eight reference documents, the field investigation files, the debriefing records and the case reviews amount to, DIA has them. That makes DIA a custody node on this map regardless of what one concludes about the underlying phenomenon.

The people matter. James T. Lacatski, a career DIA propulsion and missile intelligence specialist, was the programme manager who brought the subject to Senator Reid and who converted the contractor's deliverables into Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. He co-authored Skinwalkers at the Pentagon with Colm Kelleher, the biochemist who ran the contractor's field science effort, and George Knapp, the investigative reporter who first obtained and published the DIRD title list. AARO's Volume I addresses that body of work by describing the contractor's Utah property investigations, its interest in shadow figures, creatures, remote viewing and human consciousness anomalies, and its plan to hire psychics. AARO presents this as evidence the programme lacked merit. It is equally evidence that a defence intelligence agency programme was pursuing lines of inquiry it would never have funded without something driving it.

One further fact belongs on the board. AARO states that it partnered with DIA's archives for the historical review. Yet as of the National Archives Record Group 615 page's review date of 22 May 2026, DIA does not appear among the agencies with a UAP records transmittal to the National Archives. The agency that holds the acknowledged archive of the acknowledged programme has not, on the public record, delivered it to the statutory collection.

entityDossier.narrative:
The primary document here is Gerald K. Haines, CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90, published in Studies in Intelligence in 1997 and posted on the Agency's own website. Haines was a government historian with access to Agency files. What he wrote is more damaging to the Agency's credibility on this subject than anything a critic has written.

The Robertson Panel convened in January 1953 at CIA's instigation, following a recommendation from the Intelligence Advisory Committee to enlist selected scientists to review and appraise the available evidence in light of pertinent scientific theories. The panellists had expertise in nuclear physics, high-energy physics, radar, electronics and geophysics. Their formal conclusion was that there was no evidence of a direct threat to national security and no evidence of extraterrestrial visitation. Their operational recommendation was something else entirely. Haines writes that to meet these problems, the panel recommended that the National Security Council debunk UFO reports and institute a policy of public education to reassure the public of the lack of evidence behind UFOs. It suggested using the mass media, advertising, business clubs, schools, and even the Disney corporation to get the message across. In the same breath, reporting at the height of McCarthyism, it recommended that private UFO groups including the Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators in Los Angeles and the Aerial Phenomena Research Organization be monitored for subversive activities.

That is a US intelligence agency recommending, at national security council level, a domestic public-opinion management campaign on a scientific subject and the surveillance of American civil society organisations that took an interest in it. The Agency then concealed its own role. When public pressure built for release of the panel report in 1956, Philip Strong, Deputy Assistant Director of the Office of Scientific Intelligence, refused to declassify it and declined to disclose CIA sponsorship of the panel. Haines records that the Agency instead prepared a sanitized version which deleted any reference to CIA and avoided mention of any psychological warfare potential in the UFO controversy. When Donald Keyhoe told Mike Wallace on CBS in March 1958 that the CIA was deeply involved and had sponsored the panel, the Agency held firm to its policy of not revealing its role in UFO investigations and refused to declassify the full report.

The U-2 passage is the strongest single piece of documentary evidence anywhere in the official record that the United States Government has deliberately generated false explanations for aerial phenomena and sustained them for years. Haines writes that Air Force BLUE BOOK investigators aware of the secret U-2 flights tried to explain away such sightings by linking them to natural phenomena such as ice crystals and temperature inversions, that by checking with the Agency's U-2 Project Staff in Washington they were able to attribute many UFO sightings to U-2 flights, and that they were careful, however, not to reveal the true cause of the sighting to the public. Haines adds that while perhaps justified, this deception added fuel to the later conspiracy theories and the coverup controversy of the 1970s.

The Agency also drafted, and then abandoned, a National Security Council Intelligence Directive on UFOs following the Robertson Panel findings. A directive of that class would have assigned standing intelligence community responsibility for the subject. That it was drafted at all establishes that the Agency treated UFOs as a candidate for permanent national intelligence tasking in 1953.

The modern allegations against the Agency are thinner and must be marked as such. Journalist Ross Coulthart has reported, on the basis of David Grusch and other sources, that an office within CIA has coordinated crash retrievals on foreign soil for many years. No document supporting that has been released, no named official has confirmed it on the record, and this board carries it at Tier 3 as a research direction rather than a finding. entityDossier.narrative:
The reason DOE belongs on a map of concealment has nothing to do with what anyone alleges and everything to do with statute. Restricted Data is defined by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and covers all data concerning the design, manufacture or utilisation of atomic weapons, the production of special nuclear material, and the use of special nuclear material in the production of energy. It is classified under the Act, not under an executive order. Everything else in the national security classification system flows from a presidential order, currently the 13526 lineage, and is therefore subject to automatic declassification at twenty-five years unless exempted. Restricted Data is not. It requires affirmative review before declassification, it cannot be declassified by an agency that did not originate it, and the authority is government-wide. DOE's implementing regulation is 10 CFR Part 1045, most recently overhauled by a final rule published in the Federal Register on 21 December 2018.

The practical consequence is that if a UAP incident occurred over a weapons production facility, a storage igloo, a transport convoy or a laboratory working on weapons physics, the record of it could be created as Restricted Data from the moment of its generation and would then be permanently outside the reach of the executive order declassification machinery that every UAP disclosure statute has assumed. The FY2024 NDAA's records collection provisions operate on federal records generally. They do not amend the Atomic Energy Act.

The history is dense. From late November 1948 through early 1951 a wave of green luminous objects was reported over New Mexico, concentrated near Los Alamos and Sandia and over other sensitive installations. On 16 February 1949 a conference at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory brought together laboratory director Norris Bradbury, Edward Teller, Frederick Reines, representatives of the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission and the military, and Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico Institute of Meteoritics, who had personally observed the objects. LaPaz, after interviewing more than a hundred witnesses, advised the military and the AEC that the fireballs were most likely either unconventional defensive devices being tested by the United States or Soviet reconnaissance devices. The Air Force ran Project Twinkle from 1949 to 1951 to instrument the phenomenon, never fully implemented it, and concluded the objects were probably natural.

AARO's own Volume I preserves the pattern independently. It records Captain Edward Ruppelt of Project GRUDGE noting concentrations of cases in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area, Oak Ridge, White Sands, Strategic Air Command locations, ports and industrial sites. It records that AARO interviewed five former Air Force members who served in and around intercontinental ballistic missile silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth and elsewhere in connection with a narrative that UAP sightings near nuclear facilities resulted in malfunctioning missiles and a destroyed test reentry vehicle. It records that AARO continues to investigate these cases because of their potential impact on the readiness of the US nuclear programme. And it lists DOE among the agency archives AARO partnered with.

Congress has legislated the nuclear connection into permanent statutory reporting. Section 3373(k) of title 50 requires AARO's annual report to include the number and description of incidents of UAP associated with military nuclear assets, and separately the results of consultation with the Administrator for Nuclear Security regarding incidents at facilities or assets associated with the production, transportation or storage of nuclear weapons or their components, and with the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding nuclear power stations and fuel storage sites. That is a standing legal obligation on the nuclear weapons enterprise to account, annually, for anomalous objects over its facilities.

The FY2025 report is the most recent execution of it and the number is striking. AARO received fifty reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the NRC Chairman regarding unmanned aerial system incidents near US nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, a 177.8 percent increase over the eighteen reported the previous year. Forty-seven of the fifty occurred between 1700 and 0500 local. Five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours. AARO then adds the sentence that carries all the weight: none of these incidents were reported as UAP. The nuclear complex is reporting a rising volume of unexplained aerial activity over the most sensitive sites in the country and categorising all of it, in advance, as drones.

The 2015 Pantex incident is the clearest recent case. A Department of Energy report describes security personnel at the nuclear weapons assembly and disassembly plant near Amarillo observing a diamond-shaped object in September 2015, hovering and moving in a northerly trajectory at roughly ten to fifteen miles per hour, described by witnesses as around four feet tall and two feet wide at the base and thinner at the top, with conflicting colour descriptions. The object was tracked by ground radar and photographed from a nearby radar tower, and the imagery was analysed by DOE's Sandia National Laboratories. The report was released in more complete form during the 2026 executive-branch disclosure tranches after earlier heavily redacted releases.

Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, listed the Department of Energy among the White House, CIA, NASA and the Pentagon as agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading to unchecked power and corruption. As of the National Archives collection page's 22 May 2026 review, DOE had no transmittal listed in Record Group 615.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection is a statutory records collection at the National Archives and Records Administration, created by sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act and codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note. NARA established it as Record Group 615. Every federal agency was required to review, identify and organise its UAP records for disclosure and transmission, and to transfer publicly releasable digital copies in advance of 30 September 2025.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The collection is the concealment argument reduced to an inventory problem, and the inventory is nearly empty. Congress wrote a statutory definition that expressly reaches records concerning technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence, which is a legislature drafting for the existence of the thing rather than the possibility of it. It then stripped out the two provisions that would have given the statute teeth, the eminent domain power over privately held recovered material and the independent Review Board modelled on the JFK Act, leaving agencies to grade their own homework. What arrived is the measure of what compliance is worth: as of May 2026 the collection listed transmittals from seven organisations, none of them a military department, and on 28 August 2026 the Department of the Air Force became the eighth and the first service to transfer in its own right. The Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the Defense Intelligence Agency, NASA, the Army and the Navy are still not among them. A parallel executive-branch release channel opened in 2026 that routes disclosures around the statutory collection entirely.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act, sponsored by Senators Schumer and Rounds, passed the Senate in July 2023 as an amendment to the FY2024 NDAA. In its Senate form it would have created an independent Review Board with authority over agency withholding decisions, and it would have directed the federal government to exercise eminent domain over any recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private persons or entities. Neither survived conference. What was enacted in Public Law 118-31 on 22 December 2023 was the records collection framework alone.

What survived is still remarkable as legislative drafting. The statute directs NARA to build a collection consisting of copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence, or equivalent subjects by any other name, with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects. Congress wrote three categories into federal records law. Unidentified anomalous phenomena is the neutral one. Technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence are not neutral at all; they are the categories a legacy recovery programme would generate. The clause about equivalent subjects by any other name is anti-evasion drafting aimed at codeword renaming. The exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects is there to keep routine drone and balloon traffic out. Legislatures do not build statutory taxonomies for things they believe do not exist.

NARA implemented it. It established Record Group 615, issued guidance to agencies through memoranda AC 26.2024 and AC 04.2025, and set the mechanics: agencies identify all UAP records in any format, make digital copies, attach prescribed metadata, and transfer. NARA accepts only digital versions. Agencies were to complete identification and organisation by 20 October 2024 and to initiate transfer in advance of 30 September 2025. One provision deserves particular attention. Where a publicly releasable record includes redactions, the agency must simultaneously transfer redacted and unredacted copies to NARA. The National Archives therefore holds unredacted originals of redacted UAP records that it does not publish, which makes NARA itself a custody node with material it is sitting on.

The results are the story. As of the Record Group 615 page's stated review date of 22 May 2026, the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations: the Federal Aviation Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the National Security Agency, the Department of State and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. That list is as notable for its absences as its contents. The Central Intelligence Agency, whose own historian documented decades of UFO cover story management, is absent. The Department of Energy, which holds the nuclear complex and the Restricted Data authority, is absent. The Defense Intelligence Agency, which AARO has confirmed holds the AAWSAP archive, is absent. NASA is absent. The Departments of the Army and Navy are absent. The Department of the Air Force was absent too until 28 August 2026, when it transferred thirty records as catalog series 656595571 -- the first military department to appear in the collection in its own right, and the service that ran Project SIGN, Project GRUDGE and Project Blue Book. AARO itself, whose Volume I lists partnering with the National Archives on locating UAP data as one of its four lines of effort, appears only through OSD.

The statutory architecture explains why. The Act imposes an obligation on agencies to identify their own records and to decide what is publicly releasable. There is no Review Board, no independent adjudicator of withholding, and no penalty for a null return. Independent tracking of the transfer deadline found that most agencies approached with records requests either produced nothing or did not respond at all. A statute that asks the holders of a secret to declare it, and provides no mechanism when they do not, produces exactly the collection that exists.

The 2026 development compounds rather than fixes this. A presidential directive in February 2026 launched a multiagency effort to identify, review, declassify and publicly release UAP records, with a centralised repository opened in May 2026 on the Department of War's own website and material issued in periodic tranches. The releases have included previously unseen material, including a Department of Energy report on a 2015 incident over the Pantex nuclear weapons plant. But the channel is executive, discretionary, and controlled by the departments whose compliance with the statutory channel was the problem. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation made the point directly in February 2026, noting that Congress had already passed laws establishing a public UAP records collection at the National Archives and that the existing statutory framework gave the administration a path it was not using, while warning that classification nuances could produce misleadingly partial or incomplete disclosures.

The collection is therefore best understood on this board as an instrument that works and a compliance record that does not. The statute is the strongest UAP disclosure law ever enacted and it names the categories precisely. Record Group 615 is real, it is growing, and NARA is holding unredacted copies the public cannot see. Eight agencies have delivered, the eighth on 28 August 2026. The agencies at the centre of the argument still have not, and the Air Force transfer costs them their best remaining excuse: a military department has now done it.

claims.text: Section 1841(a)(1)(C) provides that the Collection 'shall consist of record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).'

Section 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office to review, identify and organise every UAP record in its custody for public disclosure and transmission to the Archivist not later than 300 days after December 22, 2023.
Section 1842(a)(2)(A) provides that 'No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way.'
Section 1842(a)(2)(B) bars any UAP record made available or disclosed to the public before December 22, 2023 from being withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified.

Section 1842(c)(2)(G)(ii) directs agencies to give precedence to 'the identification, review, and transmission of all records that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.'

Section 1843(a) permits postponement of disclosure only where 'the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of enumerated harms; the enacted subtitle establishes no independent review board to adjudicate those determinations.

Section 1842(g)(2)(B) requires that every continued postponement carry 'an unclassified written description of the reason for such continued postponement relevant to these specific records,' provided to the Archivist and published in the Federal Register.

Section 1842(g)(2)(D) requires each UAP record to be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation unless the President certifies that continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm whose gravity outweighs the public interest in disclosure.

Section 1841(d)(2) requires NARA's National Security Program Office, with the Information Security Oversight Office, to establish a security programme for postponed records, and section 1842(f) provides that postponed records are held by the originating body until that programme exists -- so withheld records physically remain with the agency that withheld them.

Related serials in the same index cover a request for a statement from Richard Harkins, a Western Union message from H. Dahl, TWX 150 on the crashed B-25, and newspaper clippings on the B-25 crash at Kelso, Washington.

The Fourth Air Force 1947 index carries multiple serials of correspondence to and from Kenneth Arnold, including serial 4, an investigation of 'K.M. Arnold, Flying Disc first rept in this area' sent by Headquarters Fourth Air Force to AAF and ADC on 18 July 1947, and serial 9, a 22 July 1947 request from R.A. Palmer of Ventura Press, Evanston, Illinois, for an article about flying saucers from Arnold.

Item 342UAP00024, catalogued only as 'I Once Saw A Flying Saucer - Project Blue Book, April 18, 1966', is a piece titled 'I Once Saw a Flying Saucer' by Ira C. Eaker. The catalog record does not name him. It opens on the 5 April 1966 appearance of Secretary of the Air Force Harold Brown and Chief of Staff General J.P. McConnell before the House Armed Services Committee, and states that in eighteen years more than 10,000 UFO sightings had been investigated with 663 listed as unexplained.

The Air Force RG 615 series runs to 8,093 pages across its 30 PDFs. The scans carry no OCR text layer: the only machine-readable text in the files is the page-header identifier stamped on each page during processing, so the series cannot be full-text searched as released.

Four of the 30 items carry a processing page-header identifier that belongs to a different record. Items 342UAP00003 (own identifier 00124399), 342UAP00004 (00174934) and 342UAP00007 (00423077) are all stamped 00105830, which is the identifier of item 342UAP00002; item 342UAP00027 (01030308) is stamped 01030306, the identifier of item 342UAP00026. In item 342UAP00003 the correct identifier appears only on a physical label photographed on the page. Page-level stamps in this series are therefore not reliable for provenance.

Item 342UAP00013, catalogued as '78th Fighter Wing, December, 1964', is the history of the 78th Fighter Wing (Air Defense) at Hamilton AFB, California, under the 28th Air Division (SAGE), Air Defense Command, commanded by Colonel Charles D. Chitty Jr., flying 21 F-101B and 2 F-101F interceptors. It is an air-defence interceptor wing, that is, one of the units that would actually be scrambled against an unidentified radar track.

Item 342UAP00014, catalogued as '95th Bombardment Wing History, March, 1960', is the history of the 95th Bombardment Wing (Heavy), 1-31 March 1960, assigned to Fifteenth Air Force, Strategic Air Command, permanently stationed at Biggs Air Force Base, El Paso, Texas. A nuclear bomber wing history is in the Air Force's UAP records transfer.

The 95th Bombardment Wing history was originally classified SECRET under AFR 205-1 and its title page carries the declassification stamp 'DECLASSIFIED AF/SPIB LTR, 2 NOV 79 BY AFSHRC DATE: 13 DEC 1982'. It was therefore declassified some forty-four years before it was accessioned into Record Group 615, where item 342UAP00005 carries a 5 May 2025 Air Force Declassification Office action under the FY24 NDAA. The transfer mixes newly declassified material with material declassified decades earlier, so accession into RG 615 is not evidence that a record was previously withheld.
